::: {.lead}
The previous lesson described the parts of a computing system in general.
This lesson follows one game on real devices: how it arrives on a phone, what
happens between the tap on its icon and the first frame, how the processor,
the graphics processor and the display share the work of every frame, and
what changes when the game is computed far away in a data centre. It ends by
comparing the devices that students actually play on.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary app-package install process loading frame-rate refresh-rate resolution latency bandwidth cloud-gaming thermal-throttling >}}

## 2.1 From the store to the first frame

A mobile game is distributed as a single **app package**: an archive that
contains the compiled code, the assets (images, models, sounds, levels) and a
description of the app. On Android the developer uploads an *Android App
Bundle* (AAB) to Google Play, which generates an optimised *APK* for each
device; on iOS the package is an *IPA* distributed through the App Store.

**Installation** copies the package to the device's flash storage and
registers the app with the operating system. Nothing runs yet: an installed
game occupies storage but no memory.

When the player taps the icon, the operating system **launches** the game:

1. it creates a **process** — a program in execution, with its own protected
   region of memory;
2. it **loads** the game's code from storage into main memory, so that the CPU
   can fetch its instructions;
3. the game starts its engine and loads the assets of the first scene;
4. the game loop begins, and the first frame appears.

![Launching a game: the operating system creates a process and copies code and assets from storage into memory.](images/launch.png){#fig-launch width=88%}

The loading screen that the player sees during steps 2 and 3 exists because
storage is far slower than memory. Flash storage in a phone reads from about
100 MB/s in budget models to well over 1 GB/s in flagships, while main memory
transfers tens of gigabytes per second.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.1 — Why loading takes longer on a cheap phone"}
The first level of a game needs 1.5 GB of assets. Phone A reads its storage at
1500 MB/s; phone B at 150 MB/s.

1. Phone A: $1500 \text{ MB} / 1500 \text{ MB/s} = 1$ s.
2. Phone B: $1500 \text{ MB} / 150 \text{ MB/s} = 10$ s.
3. The same game, the same level: a tenfold difference in loading time,
   caused only by the speed of the storage. Developers therefore split
   content into smaller pieces and load them while the player is busy.
:::

Memory is limited too. When the player switches to another app, the game's
process is paused in the background. If memory runs short, the operating
system **terminates** background processes to free it — which is why a game
sometimes restarts from its title screen when the player returns to it.
Games save their state when they are sent to the background for this reason.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Believing that a large *storage* makes a game start faster. Storage capacity
decides how many games fit; storage *speed* decides how fast they load; the
amount of *memory* decides how much can stay loaded at once.
:::

## 2.2 The frame on real hardware

Each frame needs work from two processors. The **CPU** runs the game logic:
input, rules, physics, animation, and the preparation of drawing commands. The
**GPU** executes those commands and computes the colour of every pixel. On a
phone both are parts of one chip, the *system on a chip* (week 4). The two
work as an assembly line: while the GPU draws frame $n$, the CPU already
prepares frame $n+1$. The slower of the two therefore sets the frame time
(@fig-pipeline).

![The CPU and the GPU work on consecutive frames in parallel; the slower one sets the pace.](images/cpu-gpu-pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline width=94%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.1 — Frame rate, refresh rate and resolution"}
The **frame rate** is the number of new images the game produces per second.
The **refresh rate** is the number of times per second the display redraws
its image (60, 90, 120 Hz). The **resolution** is the number of pixels,
width × height. The player sees at most $\min(\text{frame rate}, \text{refresh rate})$
new images per second.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.2 — What limits the frame rate?"}
On a phone with a 120 Hz display, the CPU needs 12 ms per frame and the GPU
9 ms.

1. The CPU and GPU work in parallel on consecutive frames, so the frame time
   is set by the slower one: 12 ms.
2. Frame rate: $1000 / 12 \approx 83$ fps. The 120 Hz display could show
   more; this game is **CPU-bound**.
3. Lowering the resolution would not help, because the GPU is not the
   bottleneck; simplifying the game logic or the physics would.
:::

Resolution multiplies the GPU's work. A phone screen of $1080 \times 2400$ has
about 2.6 million pixels; at 60 fps the GPU must compute
$2.6 \times 10^6 \times 60 \approx 156$ million pixel colours per second, and
twice as many at 120 fps. Many games therefore render the 3D scene at a lower
internal resolution and scale it up to the screen.

Finally, a phone has no fan. Sustained heavy work heats the chip, and to
protect it the system lowers the processor clock — **thermal throttling**. A
game that runs at 60 fps for the first five minutes may fall to 40 fps after
twenty. Developers test for *sustained* performance, not only for the first
minute, and the battery drain of a game is part of its quality.

## 2.3 Where the game is computed

Not every game is computed only on the player's device. Three arrangements
are common (@fig-where):

- **local** play: all processing happens on the device;
- **online** play (*client–server*): each device runs the game, while a
  server keeps the shared state of the match — positions, scores, the result —
  and sends updates to every player;
- **cloud gaming** (*game streaming*): the game runs entirely on a server in a
  data centre; the device only sends the player's inputs and plays the video
  stream it receives back.

![Three ways to run a game: local, client–server and cloud gaming.](images/where-game-runs.png){#fig-where width=94%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.2 — Latency and bandwidth"}
**Latency** is the delay between an action and its visible result, measured
in milliseconds; in games it is often called *input lag*. **Bandwidth** is the
amount of data a connection can carry per second, measured in megabits per
second (Mbit/s).
:::

Cloud gaming turns a cheap phone into a powerful console, but it adds two
costs. It needs bandwidth — a 1080p stream at 60 fps typically requires on the
order of 10–20 Mbit/s — and it adds latency, because every input travels to
the data centre and every frame travels back.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.3 — Adding up the input lag"}
Estimate the delay between a tap and the visible jump.

1. Local play: touch sampling ≈ 10 ms + one frame of processing at 60 fps
   ≈ 17 ms + display ≈ 17 ms: about **44 ms**.
2. Cloud gaming adds the network round trip (≈ 40 ms on a good connection)
   and the encoding and decoding of the video (≈ 15 ms): about
   44 + 40 + 15 = **99 ms**.
3. Around 100 ms the delay becomes noticeable in fast games — a rhythm game or
   a fighting game suffers; a card game or a puzzle game does not.
:::

The mini-game below lets you feel this difference: the same jump game, played
locally and with the extra latency of a streamed game.

{{< sim file="sims/lag-lab.html" poster="sims/lag-lab.png" title="Lag Lab: play with input lag" kind="game" height="560" >}}

## 2.4 Device classes for gaming

The devices that students use differ in more than raw speed (@fig-devices).
@tbl-devices compares them on the properties that matter for a game designer.

![The five device classes on which students play.](images/devices.png){#fig-devices width=92%}

| Property | Smartphone | Tablet | PC / laptop | Console | Cloud gaming |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Input | touch, sensors | touch, sensors | keyboard, mouse, gamepad | gamepad | depends on the device |
| Screen | small, portrait or landscape | medium | large, any resolution | TV | any |
| Performance | wide range, throttles | wide range | widest range | fixed, high | server |
| Power | battery, no fan | battery, no fan | mains, fans | mains, fans | mains (server) |
| Sessions | short, anywhere | short to medium | long, at a desk | long, at home | needs a fast network |

: Device classes compared for gaming. {#tbl-devices}

A game that is designed for one class must be adapted for another: a portrait
touch interface does not work with a gamepad, a long session of an open-world
game does not fit a five-minute bus ride, and a game that needs a fan cannot
keep its frame rate in a phone. Knowing the device class of the players is
therefore the first step in planning a game — and in testing it.

## Case study: the class survey

A first-year class lists the devices its students play on: most play on
Android phones from different manufacturers and price ranges; a few on
iPhones; some on laptops; one student owns a console; two use a cloud gaming
service on a phone. The same game must run on all of them. The exercises below
and the Game challenge of the interactive lesson work with this situation.

## Further reading

Tanenbaum and Austin, *Structured Computer Organization*, 6th ed., Chapter 1,
section on the computer zoo; Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, *Operating System
Concepts*, 10th ed., Chapter 3 ("Processes"), for the process and its states.

## Exercises

1. Explain the difference between installing and launching a game, in terms of
   storage and memory.
2. List the four steps between the tap on a game's icon and its first frame.
3. A game needs 900 MB of assets for its first level. How long does loading
   take at 300 MB/s and at 1800 MB/s?
4. A player returns to a game after watching a video, and the game restarts
   from the title screen. Explain why.
5. A display refreshes at 90 Hz and a game produces 70 frames per second. How
   many new images does the player see per second? What if the game produces
   120 fps?
6. CPU 8 ms, GPU 14 ms per frame. What is the frame rate? Is the game CPU- or
   GPU-bound, and would lowering the resolution help?
7. How many pixels does a $1440 \times 3200$ screen have? How many pixel
   colours per second must the GPU compute at 60 fps?
8. Explain thermal throttling and how it affects a test that lasts only one
   minute.
9. Name the three arrangements for running a game and state where the game
   logic runs in each.
10. Estimate the input lag of a cloud-gaming session with a round trip of
    70 ms, using the other values of Example 2.3. Is it suitable for a
    fighting game?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Installing copies the package to storage (no memory used); launching creates a process and loads code and assets into memory.
2. Create a process; load the code into memory; start the engine and load the first scene's assets; start the game loop.
3. 3 s; 0.5 s.
4. Memory ran short and the OS terminated the background process; the game was loaded again from storage.
5. 70 (the game is slower than the display); 90 (the display limits it).
6. 1000/14 ≈ 71 fps; GPU-bound; yes, a lower resolution reduces GPU work.
7. 4 608 000 pixels; about 276 million per second.
8. The chip slows down when it gets hot; a one-minute test misses the lower frame rate that appears after several minutes.
9. Local: on the device; client–server: on each device, with shared state on the server; cloud: entirely on the server.
10. 44 + 70 + 15 = 129 ms: too slow for a fighting game.
:::
